# StashSage

> StashSage is a free Path of Exile 2 item price checker and trade overlay for Windows, Linux and Android.

Canonical website: https://rheinze08.github.io/StashSage/
Current version: 0.5.25
Source and releases: https://github.com/rheinze08/StashSage

## Main capabilities

- Estimates the value of rare Path of Exile 2 items with an XGBoost model.
- Shows comparable listings with a nearest-neighbor model.
- Identifies modifiers that influence model predictions.
- Supports prediction history and stash pricing data exports.
- Performs normal desktop prediction operations locally.
- Also serves the same pricing engine through a Discord bot and an invite-only public HTTP API.
- Shares collected listing data and feature matrices with educators and researchers, starting with a public rings sample.

## Setup choices and data

- Desktop: prediction overlay, saved prediction history, StashScrape and StashWatch. Work and data stay on the desktop; StashWatch requires v0.5.24 or later.
- Android alone: StashScrape prices locally with bundled models. Native StashWatch requires a signed v0.5.25 or later APK. Independent phone data stays separate from desktop data.
- Phone plus desktop through Tailscale: control desktop StashWatch from a phone browser or compatible Android app. The awake desktop runs checks and stores history; Android can cache it locally.
- Agent plus desktop through Tailscale: an HTTP-capable tool runner on the same private network can control watches and retrieve listing snapshots and watch activity. The current desktop API does not expose full model-valued StashScrape runs or prediction history.
- Tailscale does not automatically sync independent phone watches or phone-run StashScrapes. Export and transfer a saved StashScrape run to open it in the desktop viewer.
- The hosted Discord bot and pricing API use a separate service; neither requires the desktop app. Its hosted API key is separate from a desktop access token.

## Limitations

- Estimates are pricing starting points, not guaranteed sale prices.
- Models learn from current unsold public listings, which may be noisy.
- Pricing models target rare items rather than magic or unique items.
- Category support depends on available training data.
